items.definition: Heavy fuel oil, also called bunker fuel, refers to the heaviest grades of fuel oil produced by distillation. It must be heated to become liquid before use.
items.core_idea: Because handling heavy oil requires heating and careful process control, its use is largely limited to large ships and power plants, which keeps its price below gasoline or diesel.
key_points: Heavy oil is the heaviest class of fuel oil grades.
Must be heated to liquefy before it can be used, which is described as a delicate process.
Primarily used aboard large ships and in power plants due to this handling requirement.
Its limited range of uses makes it typically cheaper than gasoline or diesel.
relationships: Sits at the heavy end of the fuel oil distillation stack, opposite kerosene.
trading_implications: Narrower end-use demand (shipping, power generation) links heavy oil pricing more to those sectors than to broader transportation fuel demand.
common_misunderstandings: Not a liquid at normal handling temperatures without preheating, unlike lighter fuel oils.

items.definition: Kerosene is the lightest of the fuel oil grades, positioned between gasoline and diesel in the distillation stack.
items.core_idea: Kerosene is a light fuel oil grade that, unlike gasoline, diesel, and heavy oil, is not commonly traded as a futures contract.
key_points: Lightest grade among the fuel oils.
Falls between gasoline and diesel fuel in the distillation stack.
Uncommon to see kerosene traded in futures markets.
relationships: Positioned opposite heavy oil on the distillation stack, with gasoline and diesel in between.
trading_implications: Limited futures market liquidity means kerosene is less useful than gasoline, diesel, or WTI for hedging or price discovery.

items.definition: RBOB is a gasoline grade formulated for blending with ethanol or other additives; it is the pre-blend form of finished gasoline.
items.core_idea: RBOB represents gasoline in its state before additives such as ethanol are mixed in, distinguishing it from finished, pump-ready gasoline.
key_points: RBOB stands for gasoline blendstock suitable for mixing with ethanol or other additives.
It is gasoline prior to the addition of those blending components.
relationships: Precursor product to finished gasoline once blended with ethanol or additives.
trading_implications: As a traded futures benchmark, RBOB pricing reflects the pre-blend product rather than the finished retail gasoline.
common_misunderstandings: RBOB is not finished gasoline; it excludes the ethanol/additive blend added later.

items.definition: West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is a premium, light, sweet crude oil that yields a high proportion of valuable light petroleum products via simple distillation.
items.core_idea: WTI is the most widely used benchmark for U.S. crude oil prices because its light, sweet quality makes it especially efficient to refine into higher-value products.
key_points: WTI is a light, sweet crude oil.
Simple distillation of WTI produces a high proportion of valuable light petroleum products.
It is the most common benchmark used for U.S. crude oil prices.
relationships: Serves as the crude oil source from which the fuel oil grades (heavy oil, kerosene, gasoline/RBOB) are ultimately distilled.
trading_implications: Its role as the primary U.S. benchmark makes WTI prices a key reference point for pricing other U.S. crude and refined product contracts.
